topic: whether learning to code is still worth it with AI
headline: Learn to code and adapt vs. coding is now optional
verdict: Laz makes the stronger, more concrete case for still learning to code, framing AI as a tool that augments developers and using the mechanical reaper analogy to argue fundamentals remain essential. Hemanth is more equivocal, arguing coding is no longer a necessity and pushing people toward no-code/low-code and hybrid paths unless they genuinely love coding. Both agree the real risk is failing to adopt AI tools, not AI itself.

clash.a: Laz says you should absolutely still learn to code in 2025, calling it the backbone of robotics and automation.
clash.b: Hemanth says coding is optional in 2026, not a necessity, unless you genuinely love it.
clash.why: This is the core disagreement listeners need resolved before deciding whether to invest time learning to code.

clash.a: Laz insists on strong fundamentals like data structures, problem solving, and logic before layering AI tools on top.
clash.b: Hemanth says a hybrid person only needs moderate or intermediate coding, without deep DSA or algorithm knowledge.
clash.why: They give opposite guidance on how much technical depth is actually needed to stay employable.

clash.topic: Who should learn to code at all
clash.a: Laz addresses students, junior devs, and hobbyists broadly, telling nearly everyone in that group to keep learning to code with AI.
clash.b: Hemanth says if you're unsure whether to learn coding, that uncertainty itself is a sign you should stop and consider no-code paths instead.
clash.why: This changes who the advice even applies to -- Laz assumes coding is the default path, Hemanth treats it as one option among several.

clash.a: Laz frames coding as unavoidable and central, comparing abandoning it to farmers who refused to adopt the mechanical reaper and lost their jobs.
clash.b: Hemanth frames pure coding as just one of four viable career paths, with no-code, hybrid, and consultant roles as equally legitimate alternatives.
clash.why: One treats not-coding as a risk of being left behind, the other treats not-coding as a perfectly safe strategic choice.

agree.point: AI itself won't take your job -- failing to adapt to and use AI tools is what will.
AI is not going to fully replace human workers in tech, it's reshaping roles instead.
Coding is described as evolving rather than dying, despite popular claims that 'coding is dead.'
People need to learn to use AI coding tools regardless of their skill level.

only_a.point: Uses the historical example of the mechanical reaper displacing farm labor as an analogy for AI and coding jobs.
Cites Jensen Huang's 'coding is dead' quote and argues it's frequently taken out of context by creators for views.
Cites a specific statistic of only 71,000 junior developer roles opening in the last year.
Shares personal career history, including landing roles at an aeronautical company and a big four accounting firm.

only_b.point: Breaks the tech career landscape into four distinct paths: pure coder, hybrid, no-code/low-code specialist, and consultant/trainer.
Argues 2026 specifically marks the point where AI tools become stabilized enough for people to confidently enter the field.
Describes the 2023-2025 period as chaotic, with far more AI products launched than users adopting and giving feedback on them.
Notes non-tech companies and departments like HR and CRM are also integrating AI, expanding opportunities beyond traditional coding roles.
